Title: Acadia National Park
Trivia:
Cadillac Mountain is often cited as one of the first places to see sunrise in the continental United States for part of the year.

Acadia's coastline is built largely from pink granite shaped by glaciers and crashing waves.

Tidepools along Acadia's shore reveal starfish, crabs, and other small sea life at low tide.

Maine lobster boats are a common sight in the waters near Acadia's coastal villages.

Historic schooners still sail past Acadia's rocky shoreline, evoking the region's maritime history.

Acadia's carriage roads were built without cars in mind, designed instead for horse-drawn carriages.

Puffins nest on islands near Acadia and have been the focus of long-running conservation efforts.

Spruce and fir forests cover much of Acadia's rugged, rocky terrain.

Somes Sound, sometimes called the only fjord on the East Coast, cuts into Acadia's landscape.

Acadia's popularity for sunrise viewing draws large crowds to Cadillac Mountain, especially in fall.

Acadia's rockbound coast is one of its most photographed and iconic features.

Mount Desert Island contains the bulk of Acadia National Park's protected land.

Acadia offers an extensive network of hiking trails ranging from easy to challenging terrain.

Fall foliage draws many visitors to Acadia, as New England's maples turn brilliant colors.

Title: American Samoa National Park
Trivia:
National Park of American Samoa protects vibrant coral reefs in the South Pacific.

Lush rainforest covers much of the park's mountainous island terrain.

American Samoa's tropical climate supports dense, year-round green vegetation.

The flying fox, a type of large fruit bat, is a distinctive resident of American Samoa's forests.

The park includes land within traditional Samoan villages rather than uninhabited wilderness.

American Samoa is the only US national park located south of the equator, in the South Pacific.

Palm trees line many of the park's beaches and coastal areas.

The park protects a mix of volcanic island terrain across several separate Samoan islands.

Snorkeling reveals the vivid coral reefs surrounding American Samoa's coastline.

Traditional Samoan culture and land practices remain closely tied to the park's management.

American Samoa is one of the most remote and least visited units in the entire park system.

The park's lush, tropical scenery has earned it a reputation as a hidden paradise.

American Samoa supports unique wildlife found nowhere else in the US national park system.

Rich marine ecosystems surround the islands protected within American Samoa's boundaries.

Title: Arches National Park
Trivia:
Arches National Park's sandstone formations have been shaped by millions of years of erosion.

Delicate Arch is the park's most iconic and widely photographed natural arch.

Balanced Rock appears to defy gravity, perched atop a much narrower base.

Wind and water erosion continue to slowly reshape the park's sandstone arches.

Thin rock walls called fins often erode further into freestanding arches over time.

A natural arch forms a rock span with an opening beneath it created by erosion.

Erosion has carved window-like openings through several of the park's rock formations.

Landscape Arch is one of the longest natural rock spans in the world.

Arches National Park sits within Utah's high desert region.

Sunset light dramatically colors the park's red sandstone arches and formations.

The unique geology of the region has produced one of the highest concentrations of natural arches on Earth.

Many of the park's arches are considered fragile and could eventually collapse.

The park contains numerous distinct natural arches within its boundaries.

Several arches within the park have collapsed naturally over recorded history.

Title: Badlands National Park
Trivia:
Wind and water have eroded Badlands National Park's terrain into dramatic spires and ridges.

Sharp rock spires rise throughout the park's rugged, layered terrain.

Badlands National Park contains one of the richest fossil beds in the world.

Bison roam the grasslands surrounding the park's eroded rock formations.

Prairie dog towns are common throughout Badlands National Park's grassland areas.

Bighorn sheep have been reintroduced to the park's rugged terrain.

Colorful layered rock strata reveal millions of years of geologic history.

Mixed-grass prairie surrounds much of the park's dramatic badlands formations.

The park's rugged terrain historically made travel through the region especially difficult.

Sunset light dramatically highlights the colorful layers within Badlands' rock formations.

Paleontologists have discovered numerous ancient mammal fossils throughout the Badlands.

Large sections of the park are managed as protected wilderness.

Mixed-grass prairie ecosystems border the park's dramatic eroded formations.

Distinct colored layers of rock reveal the changing environments the region has passed through.

Title: Big Bend National Park
Trivia:
The Rio Grande forms the international border along much of Big Bend National Park.

The Chisos Mountains rise dramatically from the desert floor within Big Bend.

Big Bend protects a vast stretch of Chihuahuan Desert landscape.

The Rio Grande has carved several dramatic canyons through Big Bend's limestone cliffs.

Big Bend sits directly along the US-Mexico border, sharing its river with two nations.

Natural hot springs along the Rio Grande have drawn visitors to Big Bend for generations.

Roadrunners are commonly spotted darting across Big Bend's desert trails.

Big Bend's mountains create a "sky island" habitat distinct from the surrounding desert.

Big Bend's remote location and clear skies make it one of the best stargazing spots in the country.

Big Bend has yielded significant dinosaur and other fossil discoveries over the years.

Javelinas, a wild pig-like mammal, roam throughout Big Bend's desert terrain.

Big Bend is one of the least visited and most remote national parks in the lower 48 states.

Binoculars are essential for spotting Big Bend's diverse desert and mountain wildlife.

Big Bend's desert sunsets are famous for their vivid, dramatic colors.

Title: Biscayne National Park
Trivia:
Biscayne National Park protects a section of coral reef just off the Florida coast.

Extensive mangrove forests line much of Biscayne's shoreline, sheltering young marine life.

Snorkeling is one of the most popular ways to explore Biscayne's shallow reef waters.

Historic shipwrecks scattered across Biscayne's waters attract divers and history enthusiasts alike.

Kayaking through Biscayne's calm waters offers a quiet way to explore its mangrove islands.

Numerous small islets dot Biscayne Bay within the park's boundaries.

Seagrass beds throughout Biscayne Bay provide critical habitat for marine species.

Biscayne's warm, tropical waters support a wide variety of colorful reef fish.

Boating is essential for reaching most of Biscayne National Park, since it's over 95 percent water.

A historic lighthouse stands on one of the park's small keys.

Biscayne protects a rich estuary where fresh and salt water mix near the Florida coastline.

The park preserves a chain of marine ecosystems from mangroves to open ocean reef.

Recreational fishing is a popular activity within designated areas of Biscayne National Park.

Biscayne's clear, shallow waters make its underwater habitats especially visible to visitors.

Title: Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park
Trivia:
The Gunnison River carved the Black Canyon over roughly two million years.

The canyon's extreme steepness makes portions of it difficult to safely access.

Black Canyon gets its name from how little sunlight reaches its deep, narrow walls.

Some sections of the canyon are narrower than they are deep.

Sheer cliff walls drop dramatically toward the Gunnison River below.

Painted Wall is the tallest cliff face in Colorado, located within Black Canyon.

The canyon's dark rock includes ancient schist and gneiss, among the oldest rock in North America.

Popular overlooks along the rim reveal the canyon's dramatic depth and narrowness.

Rim Road provides access to several scenic overlooks along Black Canyon's edge.

The canyon's precipice drops so sharply that little light reaches its base at midday.

Technical climbing routes attract experienced climbers to Black Canyon's steep walls.

Black Canyon's rugged terrain has kept large portions of the park remote and undeveloped.

The Gunnison River continues to slowly deepen the gorge it carved.

Deep shadow covers much of the canyon floor for large parts of the day.

Title: Bryce Canyon National Park
Trivia:
Bryce Canyon is famous for its thousands of tall, thin rock spires called hoodoos.

Bryce Canyon's main feature is actually a series of natural amphitheaters, not a single canyon.

The Rim Trail follows the edge of Bryce Canyon's amphitheaters for sweeping views.

Bryce Canyon sits at a higher elevation than many nearby national parks.

Repeated freezing and thawing continues to erode Bryce Canyon's soft rock formations.

Bryce Canyon's rock layers are made mostly of limestone shaped by weathering.

Sunrise Point offers one of the park's most popular views of the hoodoo-filled amphitheater.

Sunset Point is another iconic viewpoint overlooking Bryce Canyon's colorful formations.

Slender hoodoo spires rise dramatically from the amphitheater floor.

Frequent freeze-thaw cycles are the primary force shaping Bryce Canyon's hoodoos.

Ponderosa pine forests border the rim above Bryce Canyon's colorful amphitheaters.

Bryce Canyon's high elevation and clear air make it excellent for stargazing.

Numerous viewpoints along the rim showcase Bryce Canyon's hoodoos from different angles.

Bryce Canyon's hoodoos display vivid orange and pink coloring from iron oxide minerals.

Title: Canyonlands National Park
Trivia:
Canyonlands is divided into distinct districts separated by deep river canyons.

The confluence of the Green and Colorado Rivers lies at the heart of Canyonlands National Park.

The Green River carves through one section of Canyonlands National Park.

The Colorado River carves through another major section of Canyonlands.

The Island in the Sky district offers sweeping overlooks above the surrounding canyons.

The Needles district is named for its tall, colorful sandstone spires.

The remote Maze district is considered one of the most rugged and hard-to-reach areas in the park system.

White Rim Road circles beneath the Island in the Sky mesa on a scenic, rugged route.

Erosion from the Green and Colorado Rivers has carved Canyonlands' dramatic terrain over millions of years.

Canyonlands remains one of the more remote and lightly visited national parks in Utah.

Numerous overlooks throughout Canyonlands reveal dramatic views into its deep canyons.

Ancient pictographs left by earlier inhabitants can be found in parts of Canyonlands.

Canyonlands protects a vast network of interconnected canyons carved by desert rivers.

Canyonlands' rugged terrain has historically made much of the park difficult to access.

Title: Capitol Reef National Park
Trivia:
Capitol Reef takes its name partly from the Waterpocket Fold, a long wrinkle in the Earth's crust.

Historic fruit orchards planted by early Mormon settlers still grow within Capitol Reef today.

White sandstone domes resembling capitol buildings gave the park part of its name.

Layers of colorful sandstone are exposed throughout Capitol Reef's rugged terrain.

Visitors can pick fruit in season from Capitol Reef's historic orchards.

Pioneer settlers established the small community of Fruita within what is now the park.

A scenic drive winds through Capitol Reef's colorful canyon walls.

Deep canyons throughout Capitol Reef reveal the region's complex geologic history.

Capitol Reef showcases some of the most striking exposed geology in the national park system.

The Waterpocket Fold is a rare, nearly 100-mile-long monocline fold in the Earth's crust.

Capitol Reef remains one of the less crowded national parks in Utah.

Hiking trails in Capitol Reef range from easy orchard walks to remote canyon routes.

Sheer cliffs rise above Capitol Reef's canyons and historic orchard valley.

Small reservoirs and streams support the historic orchards within Capitol Reef.

Title: Carlsbad Caverns National Park
Trivia:
Carlsbad Caverns formed within thick beds of ancient limestone.

A massive colony of Mexican free-tailed bats roosts in Carlsbad Caverns each summer.

Delicate stalactite formations hang from the ceiling throughout Carlsbad Caverns.

Stalagmite formations rise from the cavern floor where mineral-rich water has dripped for ages.

The Big Room is one of the largest known cave chambers in North America.

Visitors can descend deep underground through Carlsbad Caverns' extensive passage system.

An elevator offers a quick way down into the depths of Carlsbad Caverns.

Total darkness defines much of Carlsbad Caverns' deep underground environment.

Countless mineral formations decorate the walls and ceilings of Carlsbad Caverns.

Bat guano was once mined commercially from Carlsbad Caverns for use as fertilizer.

Carlsbad Caverns contains more than 100 individual mapped caves.

Dripstone formations built up slowly over thousands of years inside the caverns.

Early explorers risked significant danger mapping the depths of Carlsbad Caverns.

Carlsbad Caverns showcases some of the most striking natural cave formations in the world.

Title: Channel Islands National Park
Trivia:
Channel Islands National Park protects a chain of islands off the Southern California coast.

Isolation has allowed unique, endemic species found nowhere else on Earth to evolve on the islands.

The island fox, found only on the Channel Islands, evolved into a uniquely small species.

Dense underwater kelp forests surround much of the Channel Islands.

Rich marine life thrives in the nutrient-rich waters surrounding the Channel Islands.

Sea lions gather in large numbers along the rocky shores of the Channel Islands.

The Channel Islands support significant nesting colonies of seabirds.

Archaeological evidence shows humans have inhabited the Channel Islands for thousands of years.

The islands' isolation from the mainland has shaped their unique plant and animal life.

Tidepools along the Channel Islands' rocky shores reveal a variety of small sea creatures.

Diving around the Channel Islands offers access to vibrant kelp forest ecosystems.

The Santa Barbara Channel separates the islands from the Southern California mainland.

The Channel Islands support a distinctive marine and terrestrial ecosystem.

Rugged, undeveloped terrain covers much of the Channel Islands' protected land.

Title: Congaree National Park
Trivia:
Congaree protects one of the largest intact old-growth bottomland hardwood forests remaining in the country.

The park's floodplain forest floods regularly, which helps enrich its soil and support tall trees.

Congaree's dense forest canopy includes some of the tallest trees in the eastern United States.

Towering cypress trees rise from Congaree's dark, slow-moving waters.

A raised boardwalk trail lets visitors explore Congaree's swampy forest without getting wet.

Congaree is one of the few places in the US known for synchronous firefly displays.

Barred owls are commonly heard calling through Congaree's quiet, dense forest at dusk.

Congaree's wetlands provide critical habitat for a wide range of amphibians and birds.

Canoeing along Congaree's waterways offers a close-up view of its flooded forest ecosystem.

Congaree contains several champion trees, meaning they're the largest known of their species.

Congaree's rich mix of hardwood species has earned it recognition as an International Biosphere Reserve.

High biodiversity in Congaree supports everything from river otters to countless insect species.

Much of Congaree remains a true swamp forest, shaped by seasonal river flooding.

Congaree is home to several champion trees recognized as the largest of their kind nationally.

Title: Crater Lake National Park
Trivia:
Crater Lake formed within the caldera of a collapsed ancient volcano.

Crater Lake is the deepest lake in the United States.

Crater Lake's basin formed from a massive volcanic eruption thousands of years ago.

Wizard Island, a small volcanic cone, rises from the surface of Crater Lake.

Crater Lake is famous for having some of the clearest, purest water of any lake in the world.

Mount Mazama, the volcano that once stood here, collapsed to form Crater Lake's basin.

Rim Drive circles the edge of Crater Lake, offering sweeping views of the water below.

A massive eruption roughly 7,700 years ago led to the formation of Crater Lake.

The collapse of Mount Mazama's summit created the deep basin that filled to form the lake.

Crater Lake receives some of the heaviest average snowfall of any place in the United States.

Crater Lake's striking blue color comes from its exceptional water clarity and depth.

The purity of Crater Lake's water comes largely from rain and snow rather than river input.

Scenic overlooks along the rim offer some of the best views of Crater Lake's deep blue water.

Crater Lake fills the caldera of what was once an ancient, towering volcano.

Title: Cuyahoga Valley National Park
Trivia:
The Ohio and Erie Canal Towpath Trail follows a historic canal route through Cuyahoga Valley.

The Ohio and Erie Canal once carried goods and passengers through the Cuyahoga Valley region.

Brandywine Falls is one of the most visited waterfalls within Cuyahoga Valley National Park.

A scenic excursion railroad still runs through parts of Cuyahoga Valley National Park.

Beavers have returned to the Cuyahoga Valley after being absent from the area for decades.

Cuyahoga Valley preserves a mix of rural landscapes between two major Ohio cities.

The Cuyahoga River, once notorious for pollution, runs through the heart of the park.

Environmental restoration efforts have significantly improved water quality in the Cuyahoga River.

Historic farmland within the park is still actively cultivated under a countryside conservancy program.

An extensive trail network connects Cuyahoga Valley's forests, farmland, and waterways.

Historic buildings throughout the valley reflect its history as a transportation corridor.

Cuyahoga Valley is known for scenic overlooks despite sitting between two major metro areas.

Wetlands throughout the park support a wide variety of birds and amphibians.

The Cuyahoga River carved a gorge through the valley over thousands of years.

Title: Death Valley National Park
Trivia:
Badwater Basin in Death Valley is the lowest point in North America.

Vast salt flats cover portions of Death Valley's dry lake beds.

Death Valley holds the record for the highest air temperature ever reliably recorded on Earth.

Badwater Basin sits at 282 feet below sea level.

Wind-sculpted sand dunes rise from Death Valley's desert floor.

Mesquite trees survive in Death Valley by tapping deep underground water sources.

Historic ghost towns scattered around Death Valley recall its mining-era past.

Borax mining once drove much of the early economic activity in Death Valley.

Rugged mountain ranges surround Death Valley on nearly every side.

Much of Death Valley's floor consists of a dry, ancient lake bed.

Extreme heat can create mirage effects across Death Valley's open desert flats.

Rare wildflower "super blooms" occasionally transform Death Valley's desert floor after heavy rain.

Death Valley features dramatic elevation changes, from below sea level to towering peaks.

Surviving Death Valley's extreme conditions requires careful planning and physical endurance.

Title: Denali National Park
Trivia:
Denali is the tallest mountain peak in North America.

Grizzly bears roam widely across Denali National Park's vast wilderness.

Arctic tundra covers much of Denali's lower elevations.

Denali protects one of the largest stretches of undeveloped wilderness in the country.

Large caribou herds migrate across Denali's open tundra each year.

Wolves are among the many predators that roam Denali's remote backcountry.

Massive glaciers flow down from Denali's high mountain slopes.

Sled dogs have traditionally been used for winter travel and patrol within Denali.

Denali remains one of the most remote and least developed national parks in the country.

Denali's subarctic climate creates short summers and long, harsh winters.

Moose are commonly spotted in Denali's wetland and forested areas.

Denali's summit rises over 20,000 feet above sea level.

Denali protects a vast, largely roadless wilderness spanning millions of acres.

Just one road provides limited access into Denali's otherwise vast wilderness.

Title: Dry Tortugas National Park
Trivia:
Fort Jefferson, a massive 19th-century brick fortress, dominates Dry Tortugas National Park.

Dry Tortugas is one of the most remote national parks, accessible only by boat or seaplane.

Vibrant coral reefs surround the small islands of Dry Tortugas National Park.

Dry Tortugas serves as an important nesting site for several species of seabirds.

Snorkeling around Fort Jefferson reveals coral, fish, and even parts of historic wrecks.

Numerous historic shipwrecks lie in the waters surrounding the Dry Tortugas.

A wide moat surrounds Fort Jefferson, once intended to protect it from attack.

The park is made up of a small cluster of remote islands in the Gulf of Mexico.

A daily ferry service carries most visitors from Key West out to Dry Tortugas.

A seaplane offers an alternative, faster way to reach the remote Dry Tortugas islands.

Sea turtles nest on the beaches of the Dry Tortugas each year.

The islands were named the Tortugas after the many tortoises early explorers found there.

Fort Jefferson was built almost entirely from brick, an enormous undertaking for its remote location.

The isolation of Dry Tortugas has helped preserve both its history and its natural environment.

Title: Everglades National Park
Trivia:
The Everglades form one of the largest wetland ecosystems in the United States.

Extensive mangrove forests along the Everglades coastline buffer the land from storm surge.

American alligators are a defining and abundant species throughout the Everglades.

Vast expanses of sawgrass give parts of the Everglades their nickname, the "river of grass."

Airboats are commonly used to navigate the Everglades' shallow, grassy waterways.

The Everglades support a rare and complex mix of freshwater and marine ecosystems side by side.

Manatees can often be spotted in the Everglades' warmer coastal waterways.

Hardwood hammocks form small, elevated forest islands within the Everglades' wetlands.

Sloughs, or slow-moving channels of water, help define the flow of the Everglades ecosystem.

The Everglades support extraordinary birdlife, including herons, egrets, and roseate spoonbills.

Major restoration efforts aim to reverse decades of water diversion affecting the Everglades.

The Everglades' subtropical climate supports species found nowhere else in the continental US.

The endangered Florida panther depends on the Everglades' large, connected wild habitat.

Much of the Everglades consists of remarkably shallow water spread across a vast, flat landscape.

Title: Gates of the Arctic National Park
Trivia:
Gates of the Arctic National Park lies almost entirely north of the Arctic Circle.

Gates of the Arctic has no roads or trails within its vast boundaries.

The park protects one of the largest stretches of true wilderness left in the United States.

Arctic tundra covers much of Gates of the Arctic's rugged, treeless terrain.

Massive caribou herds migrate through Gates of the Arctic each year.

The Brooks Range, one of the northernmost mountain ranges on Earth, runs through the park.

Gates of the Arctic is one of the least visited national parks due to its extreme remoteness.

Some local communities continue subsistence hunting and fishing traditions within the region.

Wolves roam freely across Gates of the Arctic's vast, undeveloped wilderness.

Grizzly bears inhabit the remote valleys and tundra of Gates of the Arctic.

The midnight sun keeps the park bathed in daylight for much of the summer.

Gates of the Arctic remains one of the most isolated national parks in the entire system.

The park's pristine wilderness has remained largely untouched by development.

Exploring Gates of the Arctic's backcountry requires serious wilderness skills and preparation.

Title: Gateway Arch National Park
Trivia:
The Gateway Arch is a stainless-steel monument standing over 600 feet tall in St. Louis.

The Arch's stainless steel exterior helps it resist corrosion despite decades of weather exposure.

The park commemorates westward expansion and St. Louis's role as a historic gateway.

A unique tram system carries visitors up through the Arch's curved legs to the top.

The Arch stands along the St. Louis riverfront, overlooking the Mississippi River.

A museum beneath the Arch explores the history of westward expansion in the United States.

The park's design and history connect closely to Thomas Jefferson's vision for the American West.

Gateway Arch is both a national park and a national memorial in a single unified site.

The Arch has become a defining feature of the St. Louis skyline.

The Arch's design relied on innovative structural engineering for its era.

The Mississippi River flows just past the base of the Gateway Arch.

The Arch's graceful curve follows a mathematical shape known as a catenary.

An observation area at the top of the Arch offers sweeping views of the surrounding region.

Gateway Arch National Park is the smallest national park by total land area.

Title: Glacier Bay National Park
Trivia:
Glacier Bay is home to several active tidewater glaciers that calve directly into the sea.

Humpback whales feed in the nutrient-rich waters of Glacier Bay each summer.

Deep fjords carved by glaciers define much of Glacier Bay's dramatic coastline.

Massive icebergs regularly break off Glacier Bay's tidewater glaciers.

Glacier Bay's glaciers have been retreating rapidly over the past two centuries.

Sea otters are commonly seen floating in Glacier Bay's calm coastal waters.

Kayaking offers a quiet, close-up way to explore Glacier Bay's glaciers and wildlife.

Much of Glacier Bay National Park remains protected as pristine wilderness.

Glacial ice throughout the bay creates a constantly shifting, dramatic landscape.

Towering, glacier-capped mountains rise above Glacier Bay's coastline.

Temperate rainforest covers portions of Glacier Bay's lower elevations.

Glacier Bay supports abundant wildlife, from whales to bears to seabirds.

Cruise ships bring many visitors to view Glacier Bay's glaciers from the water.

Glacier Bay's pristine wilderness has been closely studied to track glacial retreat over time.

Title: Glacier National Park
Trivia:
Glacier National Park is named for the glaciers that carved its dramatic mountain terrain.

Going-to-the-Sun Road is one of the most scenic mountain drives in the National Park System.

Grizzly bears inhabit large portions of Glacier National Park's rugged backcountry.

Mountain goats are commonly seen navigating Glacier's steep, rocky cliffs.

Alpine meadows bloom throughout Glacier National Park each summer.

Glacier's namesake ice fields have been melting and shrinking significantly in recent decades.

Vivid wildflower blooms color Glacier's alpine meadows during the short summer season.

The Continental Divide runs directly through Glacier National Park.

Numerous glacially carved lakes are scattered throughout the park.

Glacier's rugged, jagged peaks were shaped by centuries of glacial erosion.

Extensive hiking trails wind through Glacier National Park's mountainous terrain.

Large sections of Glacier remain protected as pristine wilderness.

High alpine meadows support a short but vibrant growing season each year.

Glacier's remaining glaciers are receding rapidly due to a warming climate.

Title: Grand Canyon National Park
Trivia:
The Grand Canyon stretches over 275 miles long and up to a mile deep.

The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years.

The canyon's South Rim is the most visited section of Grand Canyon National Park.

Exposed rock layers in the Grand Canyon reveal nearly two billion years of geologic history.

Wind and water have eroded the canyon's walls into dramatic cliffs and formations.

Mule rides remain a popular, traditional way to descend into the Grand Canyon.

California condors, among the rarest birds in North America, have been reintroduced near the Grand Canyon.

The Grand Canyon is considered one of the finest examples of erosional geology on Earth.

The sheer vastness of the Grand Canyon is difficult to fully grasp from any single viewpoint.

Popular overlooks along both rims offer sweeping views into the canyon's depths.

Hiking into the Grand Canyon requires careful planning due to steep trails and temperature swings.

Elevation changes of thousands of feet occur between the canyon's rim and its floor.

Ancient rock at the bottom of the Grand Canyon is among the oldest exposed rock on the continent.

The Grand Canyon is widely regarded as one of the natural wonders of the world.

Title: Grand Teton National Park
Trivia:
The Teton Range rises abruptly from the valley floor without smaller foothills in front of it.

Jackson Hole is the valley that sits at the base of the Teton Range.

The Tetons' sharp, jagged peaks are relatively young in geologic terms.

The Snake River winds through the valley beneath the Teton Range.

Small glaciers persist high on several of the Teton peaks.

Moose are commonly spotted along the willow-lined waterways of Grand Teton National Park.

Alpine terrain near the highest peaks supports specially adapted plants and wildlife.

The Tetons attract experienced mountaineers seeking technical climbing routes.

Wildflower meadows bloom across Grand Teton's valley floor each summer.

Grand Teton's rugged, dramatic skyline is one of the most recognizable in the National Park System.

Elk migrate through Grand Teton National Park between seasonal ranges.

Sunrise light often turns the Teton peaks a striking shade of pink or gold.

Historic ranches within Grand Teton reflect the valley's early homesteading history.

Grand Teton, the range's tallest peak, rises over 13,000 feet above the valley floor.

Title: Great Basin National Park
Trivia:
Great Basin protects some of the oldest known living trees, ancient bristlecone pines.

Wheeler Peak is the park's tallest mountain, rising over 13,000 feet.

Lehman Caves offers guided tours through an elaborate underground limestone cave system.

Great Basin's remote location and clear air make it a designated dark sky park.

Some bristlecone pines in the park are estimated to be over 4,000 years old.

Alpine terrain near Wheeler Peak supports plants adapted to harsh, high-elevation conditions.

A small glacier persists on the slopes of Wheeler Peak despite the surrounding desert climate.

Sagebrush covers much of the lower elevations of Great Basin National Park.

Great Basin remains one of the least visited national parks in the continental United States.

Dramatic elevation changes create several distinct ecosystems within a single park.

Great Basin's exceptionally dark night skies attract dedicated stargazers.

Forests transition from desert scrub to alpine trees as elevation increases within the park.

Limestone formations underlie much of the cave system found within Great Basin.

The park's remote desert setting has helped preserve its unusually pristine night skies.

Title: Great Sand Dunes National Park
Trivia:
Great Sand Dunes protects the tallest sand dunes in North America.

Sandboarding down the dunes has become a popular activity for park visitors.

Alpine peaks rise dramatically just beyond the park's massive sand dunes.

Medano Creek flows seasonally at the base of the dunes, creating a unique beach-like setting.

Wind has shaped and piled the park's sand into towering dunes over thousands of years.

Medano Creek's flow varies dramatically depending on snowmelt from nearby mountains.

Grassland surrounds portions of the dune field at lower elevations.

The park protects a rare and unusual ecosystem combining desert dunes and alpine mountains.

Dramatic elevation changes exist between the valley floor dunes and the surrounding peaks.

The Ord's kangaroo rat is specially adapted to survive within the sandy dune habitat.

Medano Creek's seasonal flow typically peaks in late spring before drying up in summer.

The stark contrast between towering dunes and snow-capped peaks defines the park's scenery.

Wind constantly reshapes small ripple patterns across the surface of the dunes.

The vast dune field spans several square miles within the surrounding mountain valley.

Title: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
Trivia:
The Great Smoky Mountains get their name from the natural fog that often blankets the peaks.

The park hosts one of the best-known synchronous firefly displays in North America each summer.

Great Smoky Mountains National Park has extraordinary biodiversity, including thousands of documented species.

Black bears are a well-known and closely monitored resident of the Great Smoky Mountains.

A section of the Appalachian Trail runs directly through the heart of the park.

Persistent mist and haze give the Smoky Mountains their distinctive bluish appearance.

Extensive historic logging shaped the landscape before much of the area became protected.

The park is considered a global hotspot for salamander diversity.

Newfound Gap offers one of the park's most popular mountain overlooks.

A long, forested ridge line forms the backbone of the Great Smoky Mountains.

Cades Cove is a historic valley popular for its wildlife viewing and pioneer-era buildings.

Spring wildflower blooms draw many visitors to the Smokies each year.

Elk were reintroduced to the Great Smoky Mountains after being absent for over a century.

Great Smoky Mountains is consistently the most visited national park in the United States.

Title: Guadalupe Mountains National Park
Trivia:
Guadalupe Peak is the highest point in the entire state of Texas.

The Guadalupe Mountains formed from an ancient fossilized coral reef.

Guadalupe Mountains National Park contains one of the best-preserved fossil reefs in the world.

Guadalupe Peak, the park's highest point, rises over 8,700 feet above sea level.

The park sits at the edge of the Chihuahuan Desert.

McKittrick Canyon is famous for its vivid fall foliage display in the desert landscape.

Steep canyons cut through the Guadalupe Mountains' rugged limestone terrain.

Much of the park's rock is limestone formed from the ancient reef.
